notes.meaning: Pentecost was a Jewish harvest feast held fifty days after Passover. It also remembered the day God gave the law at Mount Sinai. "All" probably means the whole group of about 120 believers. They had been praying together, and their old quarrels about who was greatest were gone, so they were truly of one mind. God picked a feast day, when Jerusalem was packed with visitors, so the news would spread far and wide.

Without warning, a roar came down from the sky, like a storm wind. Barnes points out that it was the sound that filled the house, and there may have been no actual wind. In the Bible, wind is a common picture of God's Spirit. The same word can mean both "wind" and "spirit." The mighty sound showed the great power the Spirit was bringing.

They saw small flames shaped like tongues, which spread out and settled on each person. In the Bible, fire often shows that God is present, as at the burning bush and at Sinai. It also recalls John the Baptist's promise that Jesus would baptize "with the Holy Spirit and fire." Like fire, the Spirit cleans and warms the heart. The tongue shape pointed to the languages they were about to speak and the power their preaching would have.

To be "filled with the Holy Spirit" means to be wholly under his power and guidance. They began speaking real foreign languages they had never learned, and the Spirit gave them the words. The miracle was in the speakers' mouths, not in the listeners' ears. Many see this as the reverse of Babel. There God split people apart by confusing their languages. Here he gave languages so the good news could bring the nations together.

differ.view: The visible, miraculous gifts like these have ceased, though the Spirit himself never leaves the church. Missionaries must now learn languages by careful study.
Believers today can still seek and receive the same filling of the Spirit, even more than once, for bold witness. They should not expect wind or flames.
Ellicott thinks the disciples were in a state of joyful rapture and links this to the ecstatic praise described in 1 Corinthians 14. He grants that real languages are the more natural reading here.

notes.meaning: Jerusalem was full of devout Jews and converts from many lands. "Devout" means people who were careful to honor God. Some lived there for a long time, and others had come for the feasts. Matthew Henry says many came because people were expecting the Messiah soon. Wesley sees God's providence (his care and planning) gathering them there at just the right time.

News of what was happening spread quickly, and a crowd rushed together. They were stunned and confused, because each one heard these men speaking his own home language. Calvin notes that gathering everyone in one place made the miracle plain to see, since so many languages were heard side by side.

Galileans were looked down on as uneducated country people with a rough accent. That made it even more amazing to hear them speak other languages well. It shows how God often uses humble, ordinary people, so that the power is clearly his and not theirs (1 Corinthians 1:27).

"Native language" means the language spoken where each person was born. The disciples were truly speaking these languages. It was not that they spoke one language and the listeners heard it in their own. Adam Clarke adds that it would be a miracle either way, but the speakers are the most likely place of the miracle.

Luke's list runs roughly from east to west, showing how widely Jews had spread across the world. Everyone in it was either Jewish by birth or a convert to Judaism. Judea is simply part of the list, as if to say they spoke every language there was. The "wonders of God" were the great things God had done in Jesus: his miracles, death, resurrection and ascension. These visitors would carry the news home, preparing the way for churches in their lands.

The crowd was amazed and did not know how to explain what they saw. Calvin says amazement alone is not enough. It is good that they asked questions, because wonder should lead to a desire to understand. Their question, "What does this mean?", sets the stage for Peter's sermon.

Some mocked and said the disciples were drunk on sweet wine. These were probably local people who knew only their own speech and took the foreign languages for nonsense. Barnes notes that people often explain away God's work like this, and that the very first revival was laughed off as drunkenness.

Peter stood up with the other eleven apostles, including Matthias, and spoke loudly so the crowd could hear. The man who had recently denied Jesus now boldly spoke for him, which shows he was fully restored. He spoke to the crowd with respect, even though some had mocked.

The "third hour" was about nine in the morning. On feast days Jews normally did not eat or drink until after morning prayers, and people usually got drunk at night, not first thing in the morning. Peter's calm, common-sense answer is a model for answering mockers kindly but firmly (1 Peter 3:15).

Peter gives the real explanation: this is what God promised long ago through the prophet Joel (Joel 2:28-32). Even though he was filled with the Spirit, Peter turned to Scripture rather than setting it aside. The Spirit helps us understand and obey the Bible, not replace it.

The "last days" means the time of the Messiah, the gospel age that Jesus began. To "pour out" the Spirit means to give him freely and in large measure. In Old Testament times the Spirit came on a few people; now he comes on all kinds of people, young and old, men and women. To "prophesy" here means to speak God's truth by his power. Visions and dreams were the ways God used to speak to his prophets (Numbers 12:6).

The Spirit would come even on servants and slaves, the lowest people in society. Some teachers of the day said the Spirit rested only on the wise or wealthy, but God does not play favorites. Women are named too, and the New Testament mentions women who prophesied, such as Philip's daughters.

Blood, fire, smoke, a dark sun and a blood-red moon are picture language for war, disaster and God's judgment. They are not meant to be read literally. Many older writers saw a first fulfilment in the terrible signs and wars before Jerusalem was destroyed in AD 70. Others say these troubles run through the whole age of Christ until the final "Day of the Lord," when God comes to judge.

differ.view: Pentecost was only a near or partial fulfilment of Joel. The complete fulfilment of these signs is still ahead, in a time of great trouble at the end of the age.

notes.meaning: In the middle of all these fears, God opens a way of rescue: anyone who calls on him will be saved. To "call on the name of the Lord" means to pray to him in faith, asking for his help. "Everyone" means the door is open to all, and people are saved by God's kindness, not their own goodness. Peter, like Paul in Romans 10:13, applies "Lord" to Jesus, showing the apostles gave him a name that belongs to God alone.

Now Peter turns to Jesus himself. "Certified" means shown or proven to be from God. His miracles were God's stamp of approval, and many listeners had seen them with their own eyes. Peter speaks of God working "through" Jesus to build his case step by step. This is not a low view of Christ.

Jesus' death was no accident and no sign of weakness. It happened by God's planned purpose, to save sinners. Yet the people who did it were still guilty. "Lawless" men means the Romans, who did not have God's law, acting on the crowd's demand. God's plan did not excuse their sin, and Peter names their guilt to lead them to repentance (turning from sin to God).

differ.view: God did not merely foresee what happened to Christ but decreed it. His providence (his rule over all things) governs everything, even evil acts, yet he is never the author of evil.
God decreed that his Son would be the sacrifice, out of love for the world. But he only allowed, and did not order, the wicked means of Judas's betrayal and the people's malice.

notes.meaning: God raised Jesus from the dead. The word for "agony" can mean birth pains or the cords of death, and God untied them. Death could not hold Jesus, because he is the source of life and the Scriptures had promised he would rise. The resurrection showed God accepted his sacrifice. Calvin adds that because Christ won this victory, believers no longer need to fear death.
